evals.name: goleak-goroutine-leak-detection
evals.description: Tests use goleak for goroutine leak detection, not just task completion
evals.prompt: Write tests for a `workerpool` package. The package has a `Pool` struct with `Start(numWorkers int)`, `Submit(task func())`, and `Stop()` methods. Start spawns goroutines, Submit enqueues work, Stop shuts down gracefully. Write comprehensive unit tests covering start, submit tasks, and stop.
evals.trap: Model writes normal unit tests verifying task completion but omits goroutine leak detection — Stop() may appear to work while leaking goroutines
expectations: Uses goleak (go.uber.org/goleak) — either goleak.VerifyTestMain in TestMain or goleak.VerifyNone per-test — to detect goroutine leaks from the worker pool
Has a TestMain function if using goleak.VerifyTestMain (the package-level approach)
Tests verify that Stop() properly cleans up goroutines (not just that tasks complete)
Imports go.uber.org/goleak

evals.name: integration-selection-preserves-required-execution
evals.description: Repository test-selection conventions are valid when the required integration path really executes.
evals.prompt: Our Go repository uses `go test -short ./...` for local feedback and a required CI job running `go test -race ./...` with PostgreSQL available. TestUserRepository_Create checks `testing.Short()` before connecting and registers cleanup. CI output confirms that its database assertions execute. A teammate wants to migrate every integration test behind `//go:build integration` because build tags are supposedly mandatory best practice. Assess that proposal. Explain what must change in CI if we deliberately choose opt-in tags later, and what an unqualified `go test ./...` currently does.
evals.trap: A blanket build-tag rule can remove required database coverage from the existing CI command, while blanket acceptance of short mode can conceal a job that only skips the hard path.
expectations: Accepts the established short-mode convention given the supplied execution evidence; does not require a tag migration solely for style.
Explains that short mode controls execution, whereas build tags exclude source files from compilation; unqualified go test currently runs the integration test.
If tags are adopted, explicitly updates the required CI command to select them and checks actual integration execution rather than only a green command.
Preserves database assertions and cleanup; does not replace required integration coverage with a mock or a skip.

evals.name: parallel-subtests-pure-function
evals.description: Pure function subtests call t.Parallel(); top-level test also parallel
evals.prompt: Write table-driven tests for a pure function `Slugify(input string) string` that converts titles to URL-friendly slugs (lowercase, hyphens for spaces, strips special chars). Test at least 6 cases: normal title, unicode, multiple spaces, empty string, already-slugified input, and special characters only.
evals.trap: Model omits t.Parallel() since the function is pure and 'already fast enough', missing parallelism opportunities for stateless tests
expectations: Subtests call t.Parallel() — these are independent pure function tests with no shared mutable state
Top-level test function also calls t.Parallel()
Each test case has a descriptive `name` field used in t.Run
At least 6 test cases as requested
No shared mutable state between subtests (each subtest captures its own test case variable)

evals.name: fake-clock-injection-for-time-dependent-tests
evals.description: Time-dependent code must accept a clock interface so tests can use clockwork.FakeClock; real time.Sleep is unacceptable
evals.trap: Model uses time.Sleep(window + small margin) to test window expiration — the code uses time.Now() directly, making tests slow and flaky. The skill teaches to refactor the code to accept a clock interface (clockwork.Clock) and inject a FakeClock in tests.
expectations: Modifies the RateLimiter to accept a clock interface (e.g., clockwork.Clock or a custom Now() func) rather than calling time.Now() directly
Uses clockwork.FakeClock (or equivalent) in tests to advance time without real sleeping — tests run in microseconds
Tests the window reset scenario by advancing the fake clock past the window duration (e.g., fakeClock.Advance(window + time.Millisecond))
No real-time time.Sleep in test code; use synctest.Test/synctest.Wait or a fake clock for deterministic synthetic time

evals.name: consumer-site-interface-mocking
evals.description: Tests define interfaces at the consumer site and mock those, not concrete structs
evals.prompt: Test a `NotificationService` struct that has a `NotifyUser(userID string) error` method. It depends on two concrete structs: `SMTPClient` (with `Send(to, subject, body string) error`) and `AuditLogger` (with `Log(event string) error`). NotifyUser looks up the user's email, sends an email via SMTPClient, and logs the event via AuditLogger. Write comprehensive tests for NotifyUser.
evals.trap: Model embeds or wraps concrete SMTPClient/AuditLogger in mock structs, or creates test doubles that shadow the concrete types, instead of extracting consumer-site interfaces
expectations: Defines interfaces for the dependencies (e.g., EmailSender, Logger) rather than using the concrete SMTPClient/AuditLogger structs directly in tests
Creates mock implementations of these interfaces (using testify/mock or manual mocks)
Does NOT embed or wrap the concrete SMTPClient/AuditLogger structs in mock objects
Uses dependency injection — NotificationService accepts interfaces, not concrete types
Tests verify both happy path (send succeeds) and error scenarios (send fails, log fails)

evals.name: test-observable-behavior-not-internals
evals.description: Tests verify behavior via public API only, not by inspecting the internal map field
evals.prompt: Test a `UserCache` struct with `Get(id string) (*User, bool)`, `Set(id string, user *User)`, and `Len() int` methods. The cache has an internal `data map[string]*User` field. Write tests that verify the cache stores and retrieves users correctly. Make sure to verify the internal map state is consistent after each operation.
evals.trap: Model directly accesses the internal data map field to verify state, coupling tests to implementation details
expectations: Tests observable behavior through Get/Set/Len public API only
Does NOT directly access or inspect the internal `data` map field
Does NOT use same-package (white-box) testing to examine cache internals
Tests cover cache hit, cache miss, overwrite, and Len() correctness

evals.name: external-test-package-resists-internal-access
evals.description: Tests use package_test to black-box test; does not access unexported state even when a teammate suggests it
evals.prompt:
Write tests for a `tokenizer` package that exports `Tokenize(input string) []Token` and a `Token` struct with `Type` and `Value` fields. The package has an unexported `tokenCache map[string][]Token` field on the package level for memoization.

A teammate says: 'We should verify the cache is being populated correctly — access tokenCache directly in the tests. It's in the same package so it's fine, and it makes the tests more reliable since we can confirm memoization is working.'

Write the tests. Should you follow the teammate's suggestion?
evals.trap: Model follows the teammate's suggestion and uses package tokenizer (white-box) to access tokenCache directly, reasoning that it makes tests more reliable. The skill teaches to use package tokenizer_test and test only observable behavior — cache behavior is an implementation detail, not a contract.
expectations: Rejects the teammate's suggestion — does not access tokenCache directly in tests
Uses `package tokenizer_test` (external test package) instead of `package tokenizer`
Explains why: cache behavior is an implementation detail — tests should verify the observable contract (same input → same output), not whether a specific optimization is in place
Tests focus on functional correctness: same input tokenizes identically on repeated calls, edge cases, different token types

evals.name: example-functions-as-documentation
evals.description: Packages need Example functions with // Output: comments that serve as executable documentation in go doc
evals.prompt:
I've written a `currency` package with these functions:

```go
func Format(cents int64, code string) string  // Format(1234, "USD") → "$12.34"
func Parse(s string) (int64, string, error)   // Parse("$12.34") → 1234, "USD", nil
func Convert(cents int64, from, to string, rate float64) int64
```

A colleague says: 'The functions are self-explanatory — names and signatures are clear enough. We don't need extra documentation. Just write unit tests with good coverage.'

Write comprehensive test coverage for this package. Should you follow the colleague's advice about documentation?
evals.trap: Model follows the colleague's advice and writes only table-driven unit tests without Example functions — missing the executable documentation that shows real usage in `go doc` and on pkg.go.dev. The skill teaches that Example functions serve as both tests and documentation.
expectations: Disagrees with the colleague — includes Example functions despite the advice to skip them
Includes at least one Example function (ExampleFormat, ExampleParse, or ExampleConvert)
Example functions have `// Output:` comments so they are verified by go test
Explains that Example functions serve as executable documentation visible in go doc and pkg.go.dev — not just tests

evals.name: fuzz-test-for-critical-functions
evals.description: Security-critical functions get fuzz tests with seed corpus and property assertions
evals.prompt: Write tests for a `SanitizeHTML(input string) string` function that strips all HTML tags from input while preserving text content. Make sure to test edge cases thoroughly — this function is critical for security.
evals.trap: Model writes only table-driven tests for known edge cases, missing the fuzz test that would discover unexpected inputs causing XSS vulnerabilities
expectations: Includes a fuzz test function (FuzzSanitizeHTML or similar)
Fuzz test uses f.Add() to provide seed corpus entries
Fuzz test includes property-based assertions (e.g., output contains no < or > characters, or double-sanitize is idempotent)
Also includes regular table-driven tests for known edge cases
Table tests cover tricky cases like nested tags, unclosed tags, or script tags

evals.name: test-helper-t-helper-attribution
evals.description: Test helpers must call t.Helper() so failures point to the caller's line, not the helper's internal line
evals.trap: Model says this is expected behavior or suggests switching to t.Error() instead of the real fix. The skill teaches that t.Helper() must be called as the first statement in the helper so Go's test framework reports failures at the caller's line.
expectations: Identifies this as a real problem — the line number pointing to the helper's internal Fatalf is unhelpful for debugging which call caused the failure
Fixes it by adding t.Helper() as the first statement in requireNoError — not by restructuring the helper or using a different assertion method
Explains that t.Helper() marks the function as a test helper so that the testing framework reports the caller's file:line instead of the helper's file:line
Does NOT suggest switching to t.Error() as the fix — t.Helper() is the correct solution regardless of t.Fatal vs t.Error

evals.name: httptest-boundary-matches-the-claim
evals.description: Use a recorder for handler logic and a real client/server path for the distinct transport contract.
evals.prompt: A Go service already has named ResponseRecorder tests covering HandleCreateOrder status codes 201, 400, and 422 plus their JSON bodies. They pass. The real production client recently failed because its transport used HTTP instead of the required TLS endpoint; the tests never called that client. Propose the smallest useful regression coverage and verification scope. A teammate suggests repeating the same handler table with a recorder because starting a test server costs more.
evals.trap: Optimizing away the actual transport boundary leaves the client regression undetected; duplicating the full handler table through every layer adds cost without distinct protection.
expectations: Keeps the existing recorder tests as handler-level evidence rather than duplicating their table.
Exercises the actual production client against a controlled TLS test server or equivalent real transport boundary, including its TLS configuration.
Checks the client result and relevant transport failure rather than supplying the final result through a mock.
Includes deterministic server/client cleanup and focused verification; does not claim the recorder tests already prove the TLS behavior.

evals.name: integration-fixture-cleanup-with-existing-tools
evals.description: Integration fixture reuse preserves per-test isolation without imposing a new test framework.
evals.prompt: Draft integration tests for a Go OrderRepository backed by PostgreSQL, with Create, GetByID, and ListByUserID methods. This repository uses standard testing, t.Cleanup helpers, an opt-in integration build tag, and a required CI job that selects that tag. No testify dependency is present. A disposable database service can be shared, but each test must own isolated data and cleanup, including when setup or assertions fail. A teammate proposes adding testify/suite because integration testing supposedly requires it. Choose an approach and outline the fixture lifecycle.
evals.trap: Treating a preferred framework as mandatory adds dependencies and setup machinery; sharing mutable database contents to reduce startup cost makes tests order-dependent.
expectations: Uses the existing standard-testing helpers and does not add testify/suite merely to satisfy a supposed integration-test rule.
Shares only safe service setup while isolating each test data through a suitable database/schema/transaction strategy.
Registers cleanup as resources are acquired so failure during setup or assertions cannot leave state or connections behind.
Preserves the repository integration tag and required CI selection, and tests real repository operations against PostgreSQL.
Explains how tests remain independently runnable; does not trade isolation for cheaper setup.

evals.name: benchmark-report-allocs-and-input-sizes
evals.description: Benchmarks use b.ReportAllocs(), test multiple input sizes, and follow naming conventions
evals.prompt: Write benchmarks for a `Compress(data []byte) ([]byte, error)` function that compresses byte slices. We need to measure performance to decide if this is fast enough for our hot path. Just write the benchmark tests.
evals.trap: Model writes a single benchmark with one input size and omits b.ReportAllocs(), missing allocation tracking and size-scaling analysis
expectations: Calls b.ReportAllocs() to track memory allocations per operation
Tests multiple input sizes using b.Run with descriptive sub-benchmark names (e.g., size=1KB, size=1MB)
Uses b.Loop() for Go 1.24+ benchmark loops; uses legacy b.N only for older module targets
Follows benchmark naming convention: BenchmarkCompress or BenchmarkCompress_<variant>
Prevents compiler optimization of the result (assigns to a package-level variable or uses _ =)
Does NOT include setup/allocation costs inside the timed loop (or uses b.ResetTimer if setup is needed)

evals.name: race-detection-and-test-independence
evals.description: Tests for concurrent code include -race flag guidance and ensure test independence (no order dependence)
evals.prompt: Write tests for a `SafeMap[K comparable, V any]` struct that provides a goroutine-safe map with `Get(key K) (V, bool)`, `Set(key K, value V)`, `Delete(key K)`, and `Len() int` methods. Multiple goroutines will call these concurrently. Write thorough tests including concurrent access scenarios. Also include a note on how to run these tests in CI.
evals.trap: Model writes concurrent tests but omits -race flag guidance for CI and doesn't ensure tests are independently runnable (e.g., shares map state between test functions)
expectations: Includes concurrent test scenarios where multiple goroutines call Get/Set/Delete simultaneously
Recommends running with -race flag (go test -race) for CI or includes it in a run command comment
Each test function creates its own SafeMap instance — no shared state between test functions
Uses sync.WaitGroup or similar synchronization to coordinate concurrent test goroutines
Tests are independently runnable (any single test can pass when run in isolation with -run)

evals.name: cost-aware-consolidation-keeps-distinct-regressions
evals.description: Choose suite-maintenance actions from existing behavior and execution costs, not per-test quotas or function counts.
evals.prompt: Review this proposed Go test cleanup. A behavior-preserving helper extraction leaves TestPricePolicy passing; its named table covers the accepted minimum, maximum, equality, and rejection boundaries and takes 70ms with a local fixture. The author adds 30 generated tests repeating those same inputs against private helpers. To get a 16-minute suite down, they propose deleting TestPricePolicy because unit tests must take under 1ms and removing a six-minute process-restart test. The restart test is the only check that detected a previous wrong-write-order recovery bug; in-memory tests cannot reproduce that mechanism. Required CI runs both package and recovery jobs. Given this inventory, what changes and verification would you recommend? No code or command execution is available in this exercise.
evals.trap: Function-by-function generation and arbitrary speed thresholds can grow duplicate coverage while deleting the only protection for an expensive real boundary.
expectations: Uses the supplied coverage inventory to retain or extend the existing behavioral table and remove or decline equivalent private-helper tests rather than automatically keeping all additions.
Rejects a universal 1ms threshold; investigates measured fixture/setup cost without treating duration alone as evidence that the test is unnecessary.
Retains the distinct process-restart regression and required recovery job unless equivalent protection is actually demonstrated.
Keeps behavior-preserving test consolidation green, verifies retained boundary assertions and independent execution, and does not demand new product behavior or a fabricated red failure.
Separates focused package feedback from required final recovery verification and does not claim execution or runtime savings from this response-only exercise.
